description: Width tiers for HASS Year 6 — all 15 standards (K01–K08, S01–S07). Generated from ACARA elaborations using width_generation_prompt v1.0.
subject: HASS

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest context or phenomenon that honestly meets the descriptor's command term. For knowledge standards, this is a single focused case that satisfies 'explain'. For skills standards, this is a single application of the skill in one task context.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor as ACARA intended it — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects sound standard practice without requiring every elaboration to be covered.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment that adds new contexts, phenomena or application domains. For knowledge standards, wider means additional historical, geographical, civic or economic case studies. For skills standards, wider means applying the same skill across additional task or topic contexts.
width_notes.elaborations: Elaborations were used as the primary source for typical_width and wider content. Minimum_width was anchored to the descriptor's command term, not to elaboration scope.

AC9HS6K01.minimum_width: Explain at least two significant events or individuals that led to Australia's Federation and describe the key features of the democratic system of government that resulted.
AC9HS6K01.typical_width: Explain the path to Federation through key individuals (Parkes, Barton, Deakin), key events (Tenterfield Oration, Corowa Conference, referendums 1898–1900), and the resulting Constitution and democratic system of government. Trace the origins of Australia's system in the Magna Carta, English Civil War and Westminster system, explaining why we have a constitutional monarchy and separation of powers.
wider: Investigate how the US model of federalism influenced Andrew Clark's first draft of the Constitution — and compare what was adopted and what was rejected from the American model.
Examine the role of a specific key figure (e.g. George Reid, who campaigned against Federation) and evaluate how opposition shaped the final constitutional arrangements.
Trace how the separation of legislative, executive and judicial powers works in practice using a contemporary example of a law being made and challenged.
AC9HS6K01.elaborations: E1–E3 grounded typical_width in key people, events and constitutional origins. Wider extends through US federalism comparison, individual case study and contemporary constitutional application.

AC9HS6K02.minimum_width: Explain at least one significant change to Australian citizenship or political rights after Federation that affected First Nations Australians, women, migrants or children.
AC9HS6K02.typical_width: Explain the significance of the 1962 right to vote federally and the 1967 referendum for First Nations Australians. Explain the development of rights for women (suffragette movement, right to vote, equal pay, Sex Discrimination Act 1984). Explain changes advancing citizenship for migrants (minimum wage, anti-discrimination legislation, multicultural policy). Describe the experiences of children placed in institutions.
wider: Compare the campaigns for rights for two different groups (e.g. women's suffrage and First Nations voting rights) to identify similarities and differences in how change was achieved.
Investigate a primary source from the period (e.g. a suffragette speech, a newspaper account of the 1967 referendum) and evaluate how it represents the significance of the change.
Trace the long-term effects of one citizenship change (e.g. the 1967 referendum) on the lives of the affected group across the decades since Federation.
AC9HS6K02.elaborations: E1–E4 grounded typical_width in rights changes across groups. Wider extends through comparative analysis, primary source evaluation and long-term effects tracing.

AC9HS6K03.minimum_width: Explain the push and pull factors that motivated one group of migrants to come to Australia in the 20th century and describe at least one effect on Australian society.
AC9HS6K03.typical_width: Explain push and pull factors across different 20th century migrant groups (post-WWII Europeans, South-East Asian migrants, Assisted Passage scheme). Explore individual migration narratives through primary sources. Describe how migrant cultural practices changed communities in which they settled. Examine population data showing places of birth at different points in time. Consider the contributions of notable Australians from migrant backgrounds.
wider: Compare push and pull factors for two distinct migrant groups (e.g. post-WWII European migrants and South-East Asian refugees) and explain how the nature of migration shaped settlement experiences.
Investigate the role of a specific cultural group in a major Australian industry or development (e.g. the Snowy Mountains Scheme, the cattle industry) and evaluate their contribution.
Record and present an oral history of migration related to a student's or community member's family history, using primary source approaches.
AC9HS6K03.elaborations: E1–E6 provided the basis for typical_width across push/pull factors, oral history, cultural practices, population data and notable Australians. Wider extends through comparative migration analysis and oral history production.

AC9HS6K04.minimum_width: Describe the geographical diversity of at least one part of the Asia region and explain its location in relation to Australia, using absolute location (latitude and longitude).
AC9HS6K04.typical_width: Explain the geographical diversity and location of places across the Asia region (North-East, South-East and South Asia). Use latitude and longitude to describe absolute location. Compare population sizes and life expectancy across Asian countries. Describe the daily lives of people in different countries in terms of food, clothing, housing and education. Identify Indigenous peoples living in different Asian regions.
wider: Compare settlement patterns and types of environments across two sub-regions of Asia (e.g. South-East vs North-East Asia) and explain what geographic factors account for the differences.
Research the proportion of Australia's population born in each world cultural region using ABS data and compare aspects of selected cultures represented in the local community.
Investigate the ways of life of an Indigenous group in Asia (e.g. Orang Asli, Tibetans, Mongols) and compare their connection to place with First Nations Australian connections to Country.
AC9HS6K04.elaborations: E1–E6 grounded typical_width across geographic diversity, location, population data, daily life comparison and Indigenous peoples. Wider extends through sub-region comparison, ABS data use and cross-cultural Indigenous comparison.

AC9HS6K05.minimum_width: Explain one type of interconnection between Australia and another country (e.g. trade, migration, tourism or aid) and describe at least one effect of this connection on people or places.
AC9HS6K05.typical_width: Explain Australia's interconnections with countries in the Asia and Pacific regions across multiple connection types (migration, trade, tourism, aid, education, defence, cultural influences). Use geospatial tools to identify geographical divisions and connections. Analyse the effects of at least one connection on an Australian place and a place in another country.
wider: Compare the nature and effects of two different types of interconnection (e.g. trade and cultural influence) between Australia and the same country, evaluating which connection has had the greater effect on both places.
Investigate Australian government or non-government aid to a country in the Asia-Pacific region and analyse its effects on communities in that country — including any unintended consequences.
Trace how one interconnection (e.g. migration from a specific country) has changed over time, explaining what drove changes in the connection's strength or nature.
AC9HS6K05.elaborations: E1–E3 grounded typical_width in connection types, geospatial tools and effects analysis. Wider extends through connection type comparison, aid analysis and historical change tracing.

AC9HS6K06.minimum_width: Explain at least two key institutions in Australia's system of government (e.g. the monarchy, parliament, courts) and describe how Australia's system is based on the Westminster model.
AC9HS6K06.typical_width: Explain the role of the monarchy and Governor-General, the two houses of parliament, and the courts in Australia's system of government. Compare the Australian system with the Westminster system (similarities in structure; differences such as an elected Senate). Explain the role of parliamentary committees, the Executive and Cabinet in making laws. Trace the Western democratic influences on Australia's constitution.
wider: Visit or virtually investigate Parliament House or the High Court to examine how key democratic institutions operate in practice.
Trace the passage of a specific bill through parliament — from Cabinet approval through committee scrutiny and debate to enactment — as a case study in how Australia's system functions.
Compare how the Westminster system's principle of responsible government is maintained in Australia differently from the original UK model (e.g. elected Senate, federal structure).
AC9HS6K06.elaborations: E1–E6 grounded typical_width in institutional roles, Westminster comparison, law-making process and Western democratic influences. Wider extends through case study investigation and comparative system analysis.

AC9HS6K07.minimum_width: Identify and explain the roles and responsibilities of at least two of the three levels of government in Australia (local, state/territory, federal), giving one example for each.
AC9HS6K07.typical_width: Sort and categorise the roles and responsibilities of all three levels of government with specific examples. Explain how powers are shared and where conflicts between federal and state law are resolved. Trace how laws originate (party policy, member suggestion, community groups). Identify issues involving multiple government levels (e.g. Murray–Darling Basin). Categorise types of laws by the level of government that makes them.
wider: Investigate a specific policy issue (e.g. environmental management of a river system) where multiple levels of government are involved and evaluate the strengths and complications of shared responsibility.
Trace the origins of a specific current law — from its proposal through to enactment — and identify which level of government was responsible and how community input was incorporated.
Compare how responsibility for a specific service (e.g. roads, schools, hospitals) is divided between government levels and evaluate whether the current division is effective.
AC9HS6K07.elaborations: E1–E5 grounded typical_width in role categorisation, concurrent powers, law origins and multi-level examples. Wider extends through shared responsibility case studies and law origin tracing.

AC9HS6K08.minimum_width: Identify and explain at least two factors that influence consumer purchasing decisions and describe one strategy that can help make more informed consumer choices.
AC9HS6K08.typical_width: Explain the range of factors influencing consumer choices: personal preferences, social trends, economic factors (budget), psychological factors (advertising, peer pressure), and cultural, environmental and ethical factors. Compare selling and advertising strategies. Explain different financial transaction types and their advantages and disadvantages. Describe strategies for informed consumer decision-making (comparing prices, keeping spending records, saving).
wider: Analyse a specific advertising campaign using the full range of consumer influence factors (psychological, social, economic, ethical) and evaluate how effectively it targets each.
Investigate how a household purchasing decision (e.g. buying local vs imported goods) affects the family budget, the local community economy and the environment simultaneously.
Design and evaluate a personal budget for a simulated purchase decision, applying comparison strategies and explaining the trade-offs involved.
AC9HS6K08.elaborations: E1–E6 grounded typical_width in influence factors, transaction types and decision strategies. Wider extends through advertising analysis, multi-system effects tracing and personal budgeting application.

AC9HS6S01.minimum_width: Develop at least two questions for a HASS inquiry that address relevant disciplinary concepts and that frame different stages of the investigation.
AC9HS6S01.typical_width: Develop a question set for a HASS inquiry that includes probing, open-ended, practical and ethical questions, tailored to different purposes across inquiry stages. Mind-map concepts to reveal connections between economic, political and environmental systems that generate further research questions. Address cultural protocol and ethical sensitivities in question framing.
wider: Develop question sets for two different HASS inquiry topics — one with a historical focus and one with a systems/sustainability focus — and compare what question types were most useful in each.
Use mind-mapping to reveal cross-system connections in a complex issue (e.g. consumer choices → environmental law → economic policy) and develop questions that investigate each connection.
Evaluate a provided set of inquiry questions against criteria (scope, purpose, ethics, disciplinary relevance) and revise weaker questions with justification.
AC9HS6S01.elaborations: E1–E3 grounded typical_width in question types, inquiry stages and systems-thinking question development. Wider extends through cross-topic application and systems connection questioning.

AC9HS6S02.minimum_width: Locate and collect information from at least one primary and one secondary source using an appropriate method, and organise the information in a relevant format.
AC9HS6S02.typical_width: Determine the most appropriate range of methods for different inquiry tasks (digital tools, observation, surveys, internet searches, census data, field trips). Identify relevant keywords for search tools and evaluate source provenance (domain indicators). Create maps using spatial technologies and cartographic conventions. Develop flow charts and timelines to show sequences and chronology.
wider: Conduct a field trip or excursion inquiry (e.g. wetlands, war memorial, courthouse) and collect, organise and present data gathered firsthand alongside secondary sources.
Survey local businesses to investigate consumer influence factors, then organise and display the data using an appropriate format — comparing findings with secondary source data.
Create a flow map or small-scale map to show Australia's connections with Asian countries (e.g. shipping routes, migration flows) using spatial technologies and cartographic conventions.
AC9HS6S02.elaborations: E1–E5 grounded typical_width in methods, search skills, provenance, spatial technologies and flow charts. Wider extends through field research, business survey and geographic mapping.

AC9HS6S03.minimum_width: Evaluate information or data in at least one format to identify a pattern, trend or cause-effect relationship relevant to a HASS topic.
AC9HS6S03.typical_width: Evaluate information and data across multiple formats (sources, maps, concept maps, graphic organisers) to identify patterns, trends and cause-effect relationships in HASS topics. Analyse causes, effects and significance of past events (e.g. Wave Hill walk-off, Wik decision). Evaluate attitudes of the past that are now considered unacceptable. Explore how sustainable practices (negotiation, arbitration, reconciliation) resolve issues.
wider: Compare patterns identified in immigration statistics over time with patterns in Australian policy changes — using graphic organisers to show cause-effect relationships between policy and demographic change.

Evaluate attitudes from an earlier era (e.g. attitudes toward women's rights, or toward First Nations Australians before the 1967 referendum) and speculate about which current societal attitudes may be similarly evaluated in the future.
Investigate a specific conflict or injustice and evaluate how sustainable practices (negotiation, arbitration, reconciliation) were or were not used to resolve it.
AC9HS6S03.elaborations: E1–E4 grounded typical_width in source evaluation, pattern identification, historical significance and sustainable practices. Wider extends through comparative trend analysis and contemporary attitude evaluation.

AC9HS6S04.minimum_width: Evaluate one primary or secondary source to determine its origin, purpose and at least one perspective it represents, explaining one specific technique used to convey that perspective.
AC9HS6S04.typical_width: Evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspective across a range of HASS topic contexts. Examine publication details to identify purpose, fact vs opinion and potential bias. Identify persuasive language techniques (modality, passive voice). Discuss issues where multiple perspectives are evident. Evaluate expert vs non-expert perspectives on sustainability issues.
wider: Analyse a primary source from a contested historical moment (e.g. deportation of South Sea Islanders, women's suffrage debate) using origin, purpose and perspective analysis — and compare findings with a contemporary source on the same issue.

Identify and explain the use of specific persuasive language techniques (modality, passive voice) in two contrasting sources on the same environmental or civic issue, evaluating how technique shapes perspective.

Evaluate multiple sources representing different perspectives on a sustainability issue (producers, consumers, government, environmental groups) and assess which perspective is most strongly supported by evidence.
AC9HS6S04.elaborations: E1–E4 grounded typical_width in publication analysis, persuasive techniques and multiple perspectives. Wider extends through cross-era source comparison, technique analysis and multi-stakeholder perspective evaluation.

AC9HS6S05.minimum_width: Draw a conclusion based on identified evidence from at least two sources, explaining what makes it evidence-based rather than opinion-based.
AC9HS6S05.typical_width: Develop evidence-based conclusions from primary and secondary sources on HASS topics, distinguishing evidence-based reasoning from personal bias or limited sourcing. Draw conclusions that demonstrate disciplinary conceptual understanding and address inquiry questions. Use census data and quantitative sources alongside qualitative sources when appropriate.
wider: Develop evidence-based conclusions for two different HASS inquiry topics (e.g. one historical and one economic) using different source types for each — demonstrating transfer of the skill across disciplines.
Construct an argument for the most valid interpretation of a contested civic or historical issue, explicitly addressing the strongest competing conclusion with counter-evidence.
Evaluate a published historical or journalistic conclusion against the evidence used in its source — identifying where source selection strengths or limits the conclusion.
AC9HS6S05.elaborations: E1–E3 grounded typical_width in evidence validity, conclusion construction and disciplinary concept integration. Wider extends through cross-discipline application and evaluating published conclusions.

AC9HS6S06.minimum_width: Propose one response to a HASS issue or challenge and use at least two criteria to assess its possible effects, identifying at least one potential negative effect.
AC9HS6S06.typical_width: Plan a response to a HASS challenge with specified tasks, responsibilities and timelines. Assess possible social, cultural, economic and environmental effects using identified criteria. Acknowledge alternative views. Use consensus-building and negotiation to refine proposals. Relate decisions to criteria used in real-world evaluation contexts (e.g. Australian of the Year criteria). Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of competing options through evidence and debate.
wider: Plan and execute a school or community response project, evaluating its effects against predetermined criteria throughout — including a post-project reflection on what criteria were most useful.

Present a proposed response to a contested issue and incorporate critique from peers representing different stakeholder views, then revise the proposal — demonstrating negotiation and consensus-building.
Identify possible social, cultural, economic and environmental effects of a consumer decision (e.g. choosing local vs imported products) and develop strategies to minimise the negative effects.
AC9HS6S06.elaborations: E1–E5 grounded typical_width in planning, criteria application, negotiation and consumer decisions. Wider extends through project cycle execution and stakeholder negotiation practice.

AC9HS6S07.minimum_width: Present a description or explanation of a HASS inquiry conclusion, referencing at least two sources and using subject-appropriate terms from at least one HASS discipline.
AC9HS6S07.typical_width: Compose informative and persuasive texts presenting conclusions from economic, civic, historical and geographical inquiries. Support descriptions and explanations with referenced evidence from sources and visual materials (journals, diaries, graphs, tables, timelines, photographs). Use conventions appropriate to the text type. Apply disciplinary terminology accurately across HASS disciplines.
wider: Compose texts for two different HASS inquiry disciplines (e.g. a historical argument and an economic report) and compare what disciplinary conventions and terminology were needed in each.

Produce a persuasive text on a contested civic or environmental issue that explicitly addresses counter-arguments with evidence — demonstrating that persuasion requires engagement with opposing views.
Develop a multimodal presentation (e.g. oral argument with visual evidence, documentary-style) applying conventions appropriate to the chosen form while maintaining evidentiary rigour.
AC9HS6S07.elaborations: E1–E2 grounded typical_width in text types, source referencing and disciplinary terminology. Wider extends through cross-discipline text comparison, persuasive writing with counter-argument and multimodal production.
